songs.title: All I Really Want to Do
songs.note: The Byrds included it on their 1965 debut album Mr. Tambourine Man and released it as a single that summer.

songs.title: All I Really Want to Do
songs.note: Cher's version was her first solo hit, reaching the US top twenty in 1965.

songs.title: Spanish Harlem Incident
songs.note: The Byrds recorded it for their 1965 debut album Mr. Tambourine Man.

songs.title: She Belongs to Me
songs.note: Rick Nelson's country-rock version with the Stone Canyon Band brought him back to the US charts in 1969.

songs.title: The Mighty Quinn (Quinn the Eskimo)
songs.note: Manfred Mann's version went to number one in the UK in early 1968.

songs.title: Too Much of Nothing
songs.note: Peter, Paul and Mary released it as a single in late 1967, years before Dylan's own recording came out.

songs.title: Nothing Was Delivered
songs.note: The Byrds recorded it for their 1968 country album Sweetheart of the Rodeo.

songs.title: Million Dollar Bash
songs.note: Fairport Convention recorded it for their 1969 album Unhalfbricking.

songs.title: Dear Landlord
songs.note: Joe Cocker included it on his second album, Joe Cocker!, released in 1969.

songs.title: I Pity the Poor Immigrant
songs.note: Joan Baez recorded it for Any Day Now, her 1968 double album of Dylan songs.

songs.title: Father of Night
songs.note: Manfred Mann's Earth Band recorded a long, heavy version for their 1973 album Solar Fire.

songs.title: Emotionally Yours
songs.note: The O'Jays made it the title track of their 1991 album Emotionally Yours.

links.why: The Byrds put out their electric version as a single in 1965, a year after Dylan's own.
Cher turned it into her first solo hit in 1965, racing the Byrds' version up the charts.
The Byrds gave it a jangling electric arrangement on their 1965 debut album.
Rick Nelson's 1969 country-rock version was his first chart single in years.
Manfred Mann took the song to number one in Britain in 1968, years before Dylan released a recording of his own.
Peter, Paul and Mary had it out as a single in 1967, long before the basement recording was released.
The Byrds recorded it for Sweetheart of the Rodeo in 1968, from the basement demos.
Fairport Convention recorded it on Unhalfbricking in 1969, six years before Dylan's version was released.
Joe Cocker gave it a big soul treatment on his second album in 1969.
Joan Baez sang it on Any Day Now, her 1968 album made entirely of Dylan songs.
Manfred Mann's Earth Band stretched the short hymn into a long rock piece on Solar Fire in 1973.
The O'Jays recorded it as a soul ballad and named their 1991 album after it.
Its nursery-rhyme melody and question-and-answer lines are modelled on the old children's song Froggie Went a-Courtin'.
Both come out of his relationship with Suze Rotolo, the first as it frayed and the second after it ended.
Both grew out of the months Suze Rotolo spent in Italy, one a lonesome blues about her going and the other a farewell to a lover sailing away.
Both tell of American working people losing their livelihoods when the work moves to cheaper places abroad.
Both reach the fear of a nuclear war, one as a comic dream of being its survivor and the other as the end of a long roll call of wars.
Both follow a young American sent to war who comes home broken and is destroyed by what the country made of him.
Both are gospel-era songs centred on Jesus himself, one retelling his life and resurrection and the other awaiting his return.
Both are love songs to a believing woman that double as thanks for her part in his conversion.
Both draw on the Delta blues written about the great Mississippi flood of 1927.
Both take the old blues picture of a levee giving way as a sign that trouble is coming for everyone.
The second is a comic sequel to the first, a year later, in the same rambling talking-blues style.
Both are old ballads he recorded in the early 1990s that set ordinary young men against the cost of soldiering.
Both are old murder ballads in which a woman kills the man who has been unfaithful to her.
Both are old murder ballads about a man who shoots a woman and is brought to trial for it.
Both are old ballads of a young woman who dresses as a man to follow her love, one to war and one to sea.
Both are hymn-like songs of consolation that tell mourners death is not the last word.
In both the singer asks someone else to carry his greetings to a woman he has lost.
Both tell of a lady who rides away with another man and a husband who rides after her.
